analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from permanently replacing workers who join a strike.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2001 with 17 Senate cosponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, an employer can hire 'permanent replacements' for workers who join a strike, meaning strikers who offer to come back to work can legally be refused their old jobs in favor of the people who crossed the picket line. This bill would make that an unfair labor practice under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act: employers could still bring in temporary replacements during a strike, but they could not give those workers permanent status or job preferences over strikers who return or offer to return. Striking workers would keep the right to reclaim their jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who join a strike — or in airline and railroad disputes — keep the right to return to their jobs when the strike ends, instead of losing them to permanent replacements. Labor unions gain real bargaining leverage, because a strike no longer risks members' permanent jobs, which under current law is one of the biggest deterrents to striking at all. The same protection applies to railroad and airline workers under the Railway Labor Act.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to grant 'permanent replacement' status to anyone doing bargaining-unit work during a labor dispute, so a worker who joins a strike could not be permanently replaced.

It bars employers from giving hiring or job preferences to people who worked, or were willing to work, during a strike over returning strikers who have unconditionally offered to come back to work, closing a gap where companies could permanently favor strikebreakers.
It adds the same protections for airline and railroad workers under the Railway Labor Act, whose strike rules differ from private-sector workers covered by the NLRA.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with unionized workforces — including airlines and railroads — lose the ability to permanently replace strikers, a tool they can currently use to keep operating during a strike and to weaken union bargaining power. Some costs of longer or more effective strikes could be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Employers would lose the ability to keep operating indefinitely during a strike, since they could hire only temporary replacements who must give way when strikers return; some employers argue this tool is needed to keep businesses and essential services running during long disputes.
Removing the threat of permanent replacement would strengthen union bargaining leverage considerably, which employers say could raise labor costs and, they argue, prolong rather than settle disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For striking workers and unions, the benefit would be substantial: a strike would stop costing workers their jobs, which is the main reason strikes are rare and risky today. The cost falls on employers, who would lose a tool for keeping operations running during a strike and for pressuring settlements, and some of that cost could show up as longer disputes or higher prices. It does not raise wages by itself, does not cover workers who are not already in a union, and leaves every other imbalance in labor law untouched. On balance it is a real, well-targeted protection for workers on strike, with costs concentrated on the employers it targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on June 27, 2001, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
Seventeen Senate Democrats signed on as cosponsors, all from the same party and none from the other.
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill was never brought up again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in unionized industries are better off: they keep the legal ability to permanently replace striking workers, and the asymmetry in current law that the bill targeted stays exactly as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who can still replace strikers

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban permanent replacement of strikers under the NLRA and the Railway Labor Act and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 17 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original sponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 senators attached to the bill were Democrats (the sponsor plus 17 cosponsors); there is no record of any Republican support or opposition because the bill never got far enough to draw a vote.

industries.industry: Employers with unionized workforces (manufacturers, airlines, railroads)
industries.note: The bill strips away the ability to hire permanent replacements for strikers, one of the main ways employers can keep operating during a strike and pressure workers to settle. That threat is also a key reason workers hesitate to strike at all.

Unions would gain real strike leverage: members could walk a picket line knowing their jobs would be waiting when they returned, and employers could not build a permanent workforce of people who crossed the line.
